utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm slightly confused about Mr. Jasikovac, which was under number 1, because you asked who he was and then the witness told us who his father was. So, therefore, if the witness could also tell us who he was, or is there any translation problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the answer was simply not recorded. I'll repeat the question, and I thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremic, could you please tell us who the person under number 1 was, Miomir Jasikovac?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, Miomir Jasikovac was the commander of the military police company in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Under the columns 10, 11, 12, 13, and you can see the word "days" above those columns, would you say that the records under these columns reflect the whereabouts of the members of the military police company and their deployment on those particular dates?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Those records were maintained by Stevo Kostic, who was the company clerk. I was not in charge of maintaining the records. Nobody in our service was. And I believe that Stevo was very good at maintaining the records. I believe that you can tell who was absent, who was present, who was on a mission in the field. I believe that he maintained those records quite properly. I was not in charge of that. It was the company clerk who was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the crosses or plus signs? What do they mean, especially in column number 6 after your name? What do they indicate?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I suppose that that means I was present on the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the symbols for the days 13, 14, that look like a letter T?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I suppose that T stands for fieldwork.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry, just so we can follow, would it be possible to get rid of the English translation and just look at the B/C/S so we can see what Mr. Stojanovic is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could we do with the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As far as I am concerned, this is a very good proposal on behalf of my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we carry on, can I just get clarification. Witness, you said the plus sign means you are present. Present where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Present in the barracks. Present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Under 6 following your name, Mr. Jeremic, after the 27th of that month, as we can see, there are words, "work obligation." Would you please tell us Trial Chamber until when were you a member of the military police company of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: It says here that from the 27th July 1995 onwards, I was reassigned and started my work obligation. Before I was called to testify here at The Hague Tribunal, I provided an official document which indicates when I was called to work obligation, so I believe that this is correct. I can't remember the date, but I believe that the record is straight and correct. And as I've told you, even before I was called to testify, I provided a document which shows when I was called to work obligation and how long I stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I am interested in page 8 of this document in B/C/S and page 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that we will also need a part of page 6 in English, Your Honours, but I would kindly request page 5 in English first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you: In this document, you can also see the interpretation of the symbols in the document. The reason why I'm showing you this is the following. Do you recognise the handwriting of the person who wrote this? And you already identified him as the company clerk, the person who maintained the records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the witness still have to answer the question, where you've given the answer already? "Could you recognise the person of you," Mr. A, is that seriously a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is this: Do you recognise the handwriting that you see in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: No. I don't recognise the handwriting of the company clerk, but I have no doubt in my mind that this is his handwriting. I'm not sure. I don't know, but I suppose it is. I don't know his handwriting at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go back to the question -- and we will no longer need this document, I thank you. To the question about your specific duties during the 24-hour duty service at the gate of the command of the Zvornik Brigade. What specifically did you have to do there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, that was my first time at the gate but I had been briefed about the other military policemen who had already done that. They told me what to do. I told you that there were two gates; one small gate for pedestrians, and a bigger one with a ramp for military vehicles. If a military vehicle came to the gate, I would let it go. But it all depended on whether I knew the people who were in the military vehicle in question. If I didn't know them, I would stop them, I would ask them where they were headed, who they wanted to see. I would then call the duty operations officer, who would then take the matter out of my hands and proceeded from there. Pedestrians would use the small gate. They were usually soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade. I knew most of them after the three years that I had spent in the barracks so that it was no longer necessary for them to provide any ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If a military person appeared at the gate and you didn't know him and requested to be allowed to enter the building of the Zvornik Brigade command, what would have been your duty?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would stop them. I would ask them to produce some ID. I would ask them where they were headed, who they wanted to see, and then I would call the duty operations officer and I would ask them if the officer in question was there, and whether I could bring the visitor to the command. The command was only about 20 steps away from the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be duty-bound to allow that person to walk to the command building on their own or would you have to escort them?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: If I didn't know the officer in question, I was duty-bound to escort him to the building. And as for the officers affiliated with the Zvornik Brigade, that was not necessary. I knew most of them and I would allow them to walk on their own to the command building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether during your duties sometime in the evening any military personnel that introduced themselves as a security officer of Bratunac Brigade came to the gate?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember any such instance. I don't know that anybody from the security of the Bratunac Brigade arrived at the gate of my command building. I am absolutely sure of that. If you're referring to the chief of security of the Bratunac Brigade or -- I mean, Momir Nikolic, I heard of him but I'm sure that I never saw him in my whole life. During the war I was never in Bratunac, and I can claim with full certainty that while I was on duty at the gate he never turned up before the Standard Barracks. I'm sure that I did not escort him to the command to report to the duty operations officer or to see any other officer at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, did there come a moment when somebody asked for Drago Nikolic that evening? Drago Nikolic was the security officer of the Zvornik Brigade, of course.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I can claim with full certainty that while I was at that gate, nobody asked to see Drago Nikolic, chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let me move to the last topic that I would like to discuss with you. In the course of your regular duty in the course of the following days of July, did you have any specific tasks relative to taking statements from either the enemy soldiers or members of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: There was one such case. A few days after the fall of Srebrenica, my chief of security, Drago Nikolic, came to the office where we were present, and the members of a crime prevention of the Zvornik Brigade were informed by him that in the course of the day two Serbs would be brought in. He told us that they were members of the Zvornik Brigade. He said that there were grounds, reasonable grounds to suspect that they had assisted enemy soldiers, Muslims, with the intention of helping them to cross over the front line to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will stop you there for a moment because I have a question. Did that, indeed, transpire? Were those two members of the VRS brought in and interrogated?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were brought in, as well as two Muslims. Nikolic told us, before they were actually brought in, that statements should be taken from them, from all of them. Both from the VRS combatants as well as from the Muslims. He also told us that the brigade commander, Pandurevic, ordered that the Serbs in question should be sentenced to a 60-day prison term. In the Zvornik Brigade we only had a detention unit and we could only keep people for up to 15 days there, whereas a prison sentence had to be served outside of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who carried out that task in terms of carrying out these official duties and taking statements from these persons?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: It was I, my colleagues, Jovic and Bogdanovic. We took statements. I mean, we took statements from Muslim persons in terms of the Serbs having helped them to cross the lines, and all of this with a view to having those two members of the Serb brigade punished by an order issued by the brigade commander remanding them into custody for 60 days, and the statements of these Muslim persons were part of this order concerning the 60-day military detention. These statements were taken, and I think that these persons who were of Serb ethnicity were from Lokanj. I think that the name of one of them was Nesko and the other one was his son, and they described in detail how they wanted to help persons of Muslim ethnicity and why they wanted to help them cross over to the other side -- or rather, across the front line towards Teocak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm looking at the clock. We are close to the time for a break. But before we take that break -- Witness, may I take you back for a second to that evening or night when you were a duty officer at the gate of the Zvornik Brigade command. We've heard your testimony. Did you ever tell the Defence that that night a man came to you and introduced himself as Momir Nikolic of the Bratunac Brigade security organ and that that person requested to see Drago Nikolic? Did that happen during that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never said that to the Defence. Before this testimony, I had the opportunity of speaking to the Defence. Not with Mr. Stojanovic. But I never said that that night while I was at the gate the chief of security of the Bratunac Brigade, Momir Nikolic, came up to me, introduced himself, and asked me to take him to Drago Nikolic. Otherwise, I can guarantee with certainty that I have never seen Momir Nikolic. I do not know him. I heard of him. But I never encountered him. I can claim that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. We'll take a break and we would like to see you back in 20 minutes. Oh, no. Before we take that break, to whom did you speak if it was not with Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was a witness for the Defence for Drago Nikolic. I don't know what the name was of the lawyer. I think he was some Canadian lawyer. I think that was in 2009. I mean, that is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, did you speak with any member of the Defence of Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did I speak with any member of the Defence of Mr. Mladic? In relation to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In preparation of your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we had a conversation, but there was no pressure upon me. I'm telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about pressure. I just want to know whether and when you spoke with a member of the Mladic Defence team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I talked to Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I talked to him in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you never told him that during that night a man came and introduced himself as Momir Nikolic requesting to see Drago Nikolic? You didn't tell him that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never told him that a man came, Momir Nikolic. I never said that. I said to him that I did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we would like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take the break, first of all, I'd like to know whether -- and it may well be, but I have to find out why we missed that extended 65 ter summary. We as Judges. Was it sent to Chamber staff on the 25th of March? Then we have to really look into our own organisation at this moment. If that's the case, we'll verify that. Of course, Mr. Stojanovic, that new extended summary I read literally part of what was announced the witness would testify about, and the witness told us that this is certainly not what he said, and he testified today to the contrary of what is contained in that extended 65 ter summary. Do you have any explanation for this appearing in the 65 ter summary in view of the testimony of the witness over the last ten minutes? Where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I can explain, and I'll try to explain. And I said that, Your Honour, I believe that we sent the summary of this witness's statement out the 25th of March, and I believe that you should have received that too. Yesterday, when I was proofing this witness, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment, what I want to know, that we'll find out whether we missed it and why we missed it, and we have to look into that being very critical on ourselves as well. But at this moment, I am seeking an explanation as why you even again sent yesterday evening at 10.00 extended 65 ter summary in which the witness is announced to testify in a certain way, where the witness tells us that quite a while ago he had told you that this is not his knowledge, even that his knowledge is contrary to what is sent here. How does that come up in the 65 ter summary, which was again sent yesterday evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, last night when I proofed this witness before his appearance in court today, I noticed that when I wrote this summary, as I was dictating, quite simply one word was omitted in paragraph 7, "did not pass," and that completely changed the context of that sentence. And then I saw that in the summary of the 25th of March, practically, there could be a problem for me and for the witness because the witness never said any such thing. Then I informed the Prosecution and you that the witness confirmed again what he had said to me before. And then out of an abundance of caution, Your Honour, I tried to include what this witness said in Mr. Nikolic's Defence, and that's why I called this witness, because he said the very same thing in that summary in 2008. So because of this omission in the typing up of this summary, I sent this last night when I realised that there was a word missing without any other reasons, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What word is missing in the English version which so drastically changes the meaning of - and let me just look at the ... Yes. You would say: "Duty officer: No one approached upon parking a car across the street and no one came by foot nor did anyone present themselves as Momir Nikolic." Now I better understand. It's a denial in every respect of apparently something the witness may have said before. Is that how we have to understand that? Or -- because usually you do not elicit evidence from the witness that what did not happen but rather on what happened. So, therefore, I do not know what triggered the paragraph 7 to be drafted at all. It seems to be as some kind of a negation of what the witness would have said or someone else would have said. Is that how we have to understand it? That the witness denies what others have said? Is that how we have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. He is denying what others said, and he never said anything different to me. And he never said anything different from what he repeated here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apparently, that's at least how I try to understand it, that this contradicts some other evidence. Could you give us a clue as to what evidence exactly this new evidence contradicts?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he denies what Momir Nikolic says and also D301.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I now better understand where we are. It took me a while but that's perhaps also because we are a bit slow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can assist with the other task Your Honours had. The e-mail was sent on the 25th of March at 11.38 a.m. under the title: "Viva Voce Witnesses Scheduled for First Week in April 2015," and, indeed, the witness summary for this witness, as well as the previous witness, which you asked me about, are contained in the same e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And was it announced that it's a deviation from the 65 ter summary as was filed or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It says "Enclosed is the supplemented summary of testimony for the above-mentioned witnesses."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Supplemented. So there is a clue to that. That's good for us to know, and we certainly will review that and further, for ourselves, explore what happened that we missed it until yesterday evening. We leave it to that for the time being. We'll take a break and we resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Stojanovic, perhaps one question. The extended 65 ter summary in the original language, that's in your language, when was that prepared? Because it says a note in an error in the extended -- was the original also suffering from the same mistake? Or is it just an interpretation, a translation issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in the original as well, Your Honour. And yesterday I saw the error. I saw that this word was missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And who prepared it, if it weren't you? You prepared it initially?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I dictated it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when was that, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that day when we sent that. Perhaps a day earlier, because we sent it for translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you had then recently spoken to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. Earlier on I had the opportunity to talk to him. But the preparation for this was, I believe, in January, during that break. Then I saw the witness in Zvornik, and then I worked with him on these notes, and then I wrote that up. And then again here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on. How much time would you still need, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My estimate is up to 10 minutes, maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremic, we stopped at the moment when we talked about the order for you to take statements from these members of the army of Republika Srpska and these prisoners of war. You personally, did you take written statements from any one of these POWs?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take these statements in accordance with the rules on taking witness statements or statements from suspects?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I've already said about the statement and what it pertained to. I think it was proper on my side, proper from their side. They talked about what had happened, how it had happened. They said that they had lost their way, that they arrived in the village of Lokanj, near Zvornik, that their intention was to cross the line of separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The content of the statement is something that we will probably have an opportunity to see, but what I would like to ask you is the following: Did you include in the statement everything that the suspects said, exactly as they had put it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Everything they said is correctly reflected. No pressure involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Court where these POWs were put up?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, they were put up within the compound of the Standard Barracks in a military room. They were not in detention with soldiers of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, were they detained, those two Serbian soldiers, were they detained as well?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were detained. Yes, they were in custody. And then an order was written by the brigade commander. I already explained that. And they were sent to serve their sentence. Since this is an order from the brigade commander, 60 days of military detention. And in the Zvornik Brigade, there was just detention for up to 15 days. And I think they were sent to a prison with the accompanying documentation, their statement and the statements of Muslim prisoners. They were sent somewhere to Han Pijesak. Something like that. Now, I have no information as to whether they were in prison or at the front line. At any rate, they were away for 60 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time in the Zvornik Brigade, were there other prisoners there too?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were other prisoners there too of Muslim ethnicity. I've already said that this column was enormous according to certain estimates. As military policemen were saying, those policemen who had seen the column, there were about 15.000 people. Some got lost, some were late, some simply wandered off, and then some were taken prisoner. And all of those who had been taken prisoner were brought to the barracks, or rather to the Zvornik Brigade where they were put into a separate room there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to these prisoners later?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not have any precise information. However, according to the other soldiers, I had the opportunity to see that they were put onto trucks and driven away from the Zvornik Brigade. I saw these trucks. It stopped at this other entrance into the barracks. There was the main entrance where the command was, and there was another, smaller gate. There were these two trucks. And they entered there, these Muslim prisoners -- excuse me. Rumour had it that they went to Bijeljina, down there, or to Batkovic to be exchanged. I did not have any official information because that is all I heard from others. Other soldiers who were in the barracks then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge as to what happened to the prisoners of war, those from whom you yourself took statements?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know what happened to them later. I believe that they had joined the other prisoners of war and left, that they were driven away to Batkovic to a camp down there. I don't know what kind of a camp that was. In Bijeljina. I was never there. I never saw them again after that. And as those Muslim prisoners were driven away, after that there were no other prisoners of war. Nobody else was brought in. Or at least I didn't have an opportunity to see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in view of the fact that at one point you were sent to work obligation, did that also imply your physical presence in the brigade on any grounds?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: When I was sent to work obligation towards end of July, I was no longer physically present in the brigade. I was a civilian. I was absent from the brigade for two or three months and then I returned perhaps in late autumn. The negotiations had already started in Dayton, and soon thereafter on the 21st of November I believe the Dayton Accords were signed. I left the VRS and the Zvornik Brigade on the 15th of January, 1996, the following year. And I went back to my original job, the workplace that I had before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremic, thank you very much. At this moment, we have no other questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I thank you for your understanding, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Before I give an opportunity to the Prosecution to cross-examine you, I've two questions for you at this moment. Could you tell us approximately how many prisoners were taken into the barracks in order to be investigated or interviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're referring to that case in Lokanj, which I mentioned just a while ago, I believe four or five soldiers, i.e., persons of Muslim ethnicity, were brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I was referring to any prisoners taken to the barracks in order to be further interviewed and which you said that you believed that they joined the others after having been interviewed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it comes to other prisoners, I didn't have any contact with them. I did not take their statements. I don't know. I don't know how many there were. According to my estimate, when I saw them getting on the lorries, I believe that there were between 80 and 100 persons. I did not have any communication with them. I did not take their statements. I did not interview any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Hasan. You'll find Ms. Hasan to your right. Ms. Hasan is counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Hasan, if you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jeremic. Just a point of clarification for the record, you mentioned that there were four to five Muslim prisoners who were brought in in relation to the Lokanj case, and earlier today at transcript page 64, lines 13, your answer is transcribed as "two Muslims were brought in," and I'm not sure that -- it's not clear to me if that's what you, in fact, said or that's a transcription error given your current answer. We'll go over the statements, but do you remember if it was two or four or five?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: It must be a mistake in the transcript. I said the two Serb combatants were brought in and that -- I don't know. There are statements. I already provided several statements about that. I said I don't know if there were four or five Muslim -- Muslims who were brought in. I can't remember. Two Serb soldiers were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: We'll take a look at those statements, but can you tell us how long after Drago Nikolic tasked you with the assignment of taking the statements and writing up the order did you, in fact, see the father and son?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. What do you mean after? How much time? There are dates on the statements and you can see when the statements were taken. I can't remember the dates. You can look at the statements and you will see when the statements were taken. I don't know what you mean when you say after how much time did you see them. What do you mean? After the fall of Srebrenica or what? What date do you want me to tell you? In any case, it was sometime after the 24th or the 25th or the 26th of July. But they were brought in on the same day, the father and the son who were combatants in the Serbian brigade. And on that same day, those Muslims were also brought in. They were all brought in on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Was that the day that Drago Nikolic had told you to expect to take the statements and to write out the order that Pandurevic had asked for?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were brought on that same day. I was in the office when the chief of security Nikolic came downstairs to see me. He told me that I was supposed to take statements from two Serb soldiers, as well as statements from the Muslims about all the things that I've already told you about previously. I can repeat what the circumstances were that they were supposed to talk about and give us their statements about.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: We will get into this and let's just take it step by step. Who did you meet with first? Was it the father or the son? And can you tell us what took place during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I met the father or the son first. I really can't. At first they denied that they had helped Muslims. However, later I believe that Drago Nikolic hit the son. He slapped the son. And then the son cried and he said, "Dad, they know everything. Let's tell them how it really was."

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And what did they, if in summary form you can tell us, what did they tell you they had done?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: They, and I mean it was the father who did it first, found those Muslims close to their house. He spoke to them. They asked him to help them get across the defence line and go towards Teocak. In return, they promised him money. I believe that they promised him some money in return for that favour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you refer to this as the Lokanj case. Now, is Lokanj where these two, the father and the son, is that where they are from as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I believe that that's where they lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And Lokanj is in the Zvornik municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It belongs to the Zvornik municipality and it is perhaps some 30 kilometres away from the town of Zvornik itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you recall who took the statements from the father and son, if you remember today?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: You have those statements. Take a look. All the three of us were present, myself, Jovic, and Bogdanovic. I really can't remember who took whose statement. But we were all there, the three of us were all there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I understand a lot of time has passed, so let's just look at that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: 65 ter 04315, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, while waiting for the document, we have to conclude today strictly at quarter past 2.00 because there is another court session this afternoon in the same courtroom. Therefore, would you keep that in mind to stop, well, let's say, two minutes before that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, Mr. Jeremic, I know you're familiar with this document. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: We see that it is the statement of Nesko Djokic, son of Tesanj and Milka, born 1 January 1936 in D. Lokanj, Zvornik municipality. It goes on to say that he's a member of the 1st Infantry Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade. That would have been the father; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now the statement provides just briefly at the very beginning: "On 18 July 1995, I got up early in the morning to bring grass for my cattle from a field which is about 150 metres from the house. On my way there, four men appeared before me, under an apple tree. I knew immediately that they were Muslims, since they were covered with blood and also by their clothes, because they had been fleeing from Srebrenica towards their territory at that time." And it goes on. If we can -- well, at this moment, can you tell me, when they arrived at the Standard Barracks, did you -- do you recall seeing blood on their clothes?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that their clothes were covered with blood, but I remember that their clothes were torn and not in a good state of repair. But I do remember that they did not have bruises and injuries on their faces and bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you recall the father mentioning that he had provided them with food and clothing?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he gave them clothes. I know that he gave them food. He told us that. And I can see it in the statement. I can see that he asked them to give him 50 German marks to buy them some extra food, which means that he intended to bring them some more food. He didn't have the money to buy it. That's why he asked them for the money, to be able to buy them food and bring it to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So if you just look a few lines down from where the 50 marks are mentioned, it says: "Apart from food, I brought them an old shirt and torn sweaters since they had asked me to bring them some clothes." Now, I appreciate that you don't remember that, but do you have any reason to doubt that this statement was taken down accurately?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I believe that the statement was taken down accurately. I don't have any doubt whatsoever about the accuracy of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we'll have to adjourn for the day. And, Mr. Jeremic, I would like to instruct you before you leave this courtroom that you should not speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given already, or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow. If that's clear to you, we had like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom, and you may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 9th of April, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
